prompt: Which statement correctly describes the two objects created when an application is registered in Microsoft Entra ID?
choices: A global application object, and a service principal per tenant
A managed identity and an app registration, with no service principal involved
An enterprise application and a Key Vault access policy for its secrets
A service principal and a Conditional Access policy scoped to the app
correctAnswers: A global application object, and a service principal per tenant
explanation: Registration produces the blueprint and its local instance, which is why permissions are declared on one object and consented on the other. The managed-identity option is the tempting one because managed identities are also application identities, whereas they are created on an Azure resource rather than by registering an app.

prompt: What does the app registration primarily define?
choices: What the app is: redirect URIs, credentials, and requested permissions
Which users and groups have been assigned to use the app in this tenant here
The Azure RBAC role assignments granted to the app's own service principal
The Conditional Access policy that has been scoped to the application
correctAnswers: What the app is: redirect URIs, credentials, and requested permissions
explanation: The registration is the declaration of the application itself — what it is and what it would like to be allowed. Assigned users and groups are the tempting answer and belong to Enterprise applications instead, which is the governance side rather than the definition.

prompt: Under which portal blade do you govern a service principal's assigned users, SSO configuration, and granted (not just requested) permissions in a given tenant?
choices: Enterprise applications
App registrations for the app
Privileged Identity Management
Key Vault access policies
correctAnswers: Enterprise applications
explanation: Enterprise applications governs the local instance: who may use it, how it signs in, and what has actually been consented. App registrations is the closest miss and is where permissions are REQUESTED, whereas the record of what was granted lives on the service principal.

prompt: A multi-tenant SaaS app is consented to by three different customer tenants. How many service principals exist for that single app registration?
choices: Three — one service principal per consuming tenant
One — service principals are global, not per tenant
Zero — multi-tenant apps don't use service principals
Three app registrations and one shared service principal
correctAnswers: Three — one service principal per consuming tenant
explanation: Each consenting tenant gets its own local service principal, while a single application object stays behind in the publisher tenant. Believing service principals are global is the tempting simplification and would make consent meaningless, whereas the per-tenant instance is precisely what each customer governs independently.

prompt: A delegated permission is granted to an application. What can that application do with it?
choices: Act on behalf of the signed-in user, bounded by that user’s own access
Act as itself with no user context, regardless of any user’s own permissions
Access every mailbox in the tenant without any further consent at all
Bypass all Conditional Access policies automatically
correctAnswers: Act on behalf of the signed-in user, bounded by that user’s own access
explanation: A delegated permission is a ceiling, not a grant: the app can never exceed what the signed-in user could do unaided. Acting as itself with no user context is the contrasting case and is an APPLICATION permission, which is why the two are never interchangeable.

prompt: An application is granted the Mail.Read application permission. What does this allow?
choices: The app reads mail as itself, with no signed-in user, after admin consent
The app can only read the mail of whichever user happens to be signed in now
The permission is limited automatically to the app’s own home tenant
The permission needs no consent, because Mail.Read is a read-only scope
correctAnswers: The app reads mail as itself, with no signed-in user, after admin consent
explanation: An application permission is unbounded by any user, which is exactly why it always needs admin consent. The "only the signed-in user" option is the tempting one and describes the delegated form of the same scope — the scope name is identical and the blast radius is not.

prompt: Which statement about consenting to application permissions is correct?
choices: They always require admin consent, since no user is present to consent
They are consented to automatically the first time the application signs in
They never require consent at all if the application is single-tenant
They can be consented to by any licensed user in the tenant
correctAnswers: They always require admin consent, since no user is present to consent
explanation: The reason is structural rather than a matter of risk rating: with no user in the flow, only an administrator can consent on the tenant’s behalf. Automatic consent at first sign-in is the tempting invention and would make the whole consent model meaningless, since any app could grant itself anything.

prompt: An administrator grants admin consent for an application's Mail.ReadWrite application permission. What is the scope of that consent?
choices: It applies tenant-wide, to every user, not only to the granting admin
It applies only to users who individually re-consent for themselves afterwards
It expires automatically after ninety days unless it is renewed
It applies only to the administrator’s own mailbox
correctAnswers: It applies tenant-wide, to every user, not only to the granting admin
explanation: Admin consent is a tenant-level act, so the app can reach every mailbox from that moment on — which is why an unused grant of this kind is worth removing rather than leaving. Expecting per-user re-consent is the tempting safety assumption and describes delegated permissions, whereas an application permission has no per-user step.

prompt: Which User consent setting is recommended to reduce the risk of illicit consent grant attacks while still allowing convenience for low-risk apps?
choices: Allow user consent only for verified publishers and low-impact permissions
Disable user consent, and also disable the admin consent workflow entirely as well
Allow user consent for any application requesting any permission at all
Allow user consent only during defined maintenance windows
correctAnswers: Allow user consent only for verified publishers and low-impact permissions
explanation: The setting keeps the friction-free path for genuinely low-risk apps and closes it for everything else. Disabling user consent AND the workflow is the tempting hardline choice and is the worst of the options: legitimate requests then have nowhere to go, so users route around the tenant entirely.

prompt: A user tries to sign in to an app requiring a permission they cannot consent to themselves. What happens if the admin consent workflow is enabled?
choices: The user can request access, and reviewers are asked to approve it
The user is granted the permission automatically after twenty-four hours pass
The sign-in fails silently, with no way for the user to request access
The app registration is deleted automatically by the tenant
correctAnswers: The user can request access, and reviewers are asked to approve it
explanation: The workflow turns a dead end into a reviewable request, which is what makes restricting user consent sustainable. The silent failure is what happens WITHOUT the workflow, and it is the reason restricting consent alone tends to be reversed under pressure from users who cannot work.

prompt: What attack does the admin consent workflow (routing requests to reviewers) primarily defend against?
choices: Illicit consent grants, where a malicious app tricks the user
Ransomware encryption of on-premises file shares reached over SMB
Brute-force password attacks against tenant user accounts
SIM-swap attacks against SMS-based MFA codes
correctAnswers: Illicit consent grants, where a malicious app tricks the user
explanation: The attack needs no password and no MFA bypass — the user genuinely agrees, which is what makes a human reviewer the right control. The other three are real attacks defended by entirely different means, whereas none of them involves the user granting anything.

prompt: Where can an administrator review which OAuth permissions have actually been granted to an app, as opposed to only what it requests?
choices: Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions
App registrations ▸ Certificates & secrets
Key Vault ▸ Access configuration
Conditional Access ▸ Policies
correctAnswers: Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions
explanation: The actual consent record lives on the enterprise application, under Permissions, which is where an over-privileged app is discovered. App registrations ▸ Certificates & secrets is the closest miss and holds credentials rather than grants, so a review conducted there reports what the app ASKED for instead of what it received.

prompt: During a permissions review, you find an app has an unused Mail.ReadWrite application permission granted tenant-wide. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Remove the grant, since it acts with no user context and carries wide risk
Leave it, since application permissions are always lower-risk than delegated ones
Ignore it, because application permissions cannot be revoked once granted
Convert it into a delegated permission automatically
correctAnswers: Remove the grant, since it acts with no user context and carries wide risk
explanation: An unused application permission is standing tenant-wide access to every mailbox, so removing it costs nothing and closes a real path. The claim that application permissions are lower-risk inverts the truth, and the claim that they cannot be revoked is the more dangerous belief because it turns a five-minute fix into a permanent exposure.

prompt: What is the defining characteristic of a managed identity compared to a regular service principal?
choices: Azure creates and rotates its credentials, so there is no secret to manage
It can only hold delegated permissions, and never application permissions at all
It requires a Conditional Access policy to be in place to function
It can only be used by Azure Functions and by nothing else
correctAnswers: Azure creates and rotates its credentials, so there is no secret to manage
explanation: The whole difference is credential handling: there is nothing to store, leak or rotate. The delegated-permissions claim is the tempting invented limit — a managed identity is a service principal and holds application permissions and RBAC roles like any other.

prompt: A virtual machine has both a system-assigned and a user-assigned managed identity attached. The virtual machine is deleted. Complete the statement describing what happens to each identity.
template: The [[b1]] identity is removed automatically along with the virtual machine, because [[b2]]. The [[b3]] identity is unaffected.

options: it is a property of the resource rather than a resource of its own
Azure revokes every identity attached to a deleted resource
its role assignments were scoped to that virtual machine only
it holds a client secret that expires with the host
blanks.correctValue: it is a property of the resource rather than a resource of its own

explanation: The two kinds differ on one axis — who owns the identity's lifecycle — and everything else follows from it. A system-assigned identity is a property of its host, so it cannot outlive it or be shared. A user-assigned identity is a first-class Azure resource, so it survives deletion of anything it was attached to. The tempting reason for the middle blank is scoped role assignments: those do disappear with the resource, but that is a consequence of the deletion, not the reason the identity itself ceases to exist.

prompt: Ten Azure Functions apps in a fleet all need the same identity to call a downstream API. Which managed identity type best fits this need?
choices: One user-assigned managed identity, attached to all ten function apps
A service principal with one client secret shared via a configuration file
Ten separate system-assigned managed identities, one for each function app
One system-assigned managed identity, shared across all the function apps
correctAnswers: One user-assigned managed identity, attached to all ten function apps
explanation: Only a user-assigned identity can be attached to many resources, which is what "the same identity" requires. The shared system-assigned option is the trap and is impossible rather than merely inadvisable: a system-assigned identity belongs to exactly one resource, so there is nothing to share.

prompt: Build the sequence that lets a VM read a Key Vault secret with no credential stored on it. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Enable a managed identity on the virtual machine, system- or user-assigned
Note the principal ID that Azure assigns to that identity
Grant the identity the Key Vault Secrets User role on the vault
Read the secret from application code, with no credential in the code
Store the vault's master key in the VM's application settings
Create a service principal and embed its client secret in the VM's startup script
Enable Conditional Access for the VM's IP address range
correctOrder: Enable a managed identity on the virtual machine, system- or user-assigned
Note the principal ID that Azure assigns to that identity
Grant the identity the Key Vault Secrets User role on the vault
Read the secret from application code, with no credential in the code
explanation: The identity must exist before it can be named in a role assignment, and the role must exist before any read succeeds — authentication and authorization are two steps rather than one. The three excluded actions all store a credential on the machine or, in the Conditional Access case, address the wrong thing entirely: Conditional Access governs sign-ins by users rather than data-plane access by a workload.

prompt: Which Azure RBAC role is commonly granted to a managed identity that only needs to read secret values from a Key Vault?
choices: Key Vault Secrets User
Key Vault Administrator
Key Vault Reader on the vault
Contributor on the resource group
correctAnswers: Key Vault Secrets User
explanation: Secrets User is the data-plane role that reads secret VALUES. Key Vault Reader is the trap: it reads vault and secret metadata and never the value, so the workload authenticates, lists the secret, and still cannot read it — which is a confusing failure because nothing appears denied.

prompt: Microsoft's recommended preference order for workload authentication, from most to least preferred, is:
choices: Managed identity, then certificate-based service principal, then client secret
Service principal with a client secret, then managed identity, then certificate
Certificate-based service principal, then client secret, then managed identity
There is no preference, since all three are equally recommended
correctAnswers: Managed identity, then certificate-based service principal, then client secret
explanation: The order follows how much credential handling you are left holding: none, then a certificate, then a secret. Putting the client secret first is the tempting answer because it is the most familiar pattern, whereas familiarity is what makes it the most common source of expired-credential outages and leaked keys.

prompt: What does the acronym SPN commonly refer to in the context of Entra application identities?
choices: The service principal object representing an app in a tenant
A Security Policy Notification sent out by Conditional Access
A Signed Permission Notice that admin consent requires
A Secrets Provisioning Node that Key Vault uses
correctAnswers: The service principal object representing an app in a tenant
explanation: SPN is shorthand for the service principal — the local identity that receives assignments and consent. The three invented expansions are plausible only because each names a real Azure concept, whereas none of them is what anyone means by SPN in an Entra discussion.

prompt: Which statement about credential responsibility is correct for a standard (non-managed-identity) service principal?
choices: You create, store, and rotate its secrets or certificates yourself
Azure rotates its credentials automatically, with no action required from you
Its credentials are stored in Conditional Access rather than in Entra ID
It has no credentials at all and authenticates anonymously
correctAnswers: You create, store, and rotate its secrets or certificates yourself
explanation: An ordinary service principal leaves the whole credential lifecycle with you, which is the operational cost a managed identity removes. Expecting Azure to rotate it is the tempting assumption and is exactly the belief behind an outage: the secret expires on its stated date and nothing renews it.

prompt: A developer registers a new application that will later be published to multiple customer tenants. In which tenant does the app registration (the application object) live?
choices: The developer's home/origin tenant where it was registered
Every tenant that later consents to the app
No tenant — app registrations are global objects with no home tenant
The tenant of the first user who signs in to the app
correctAnswers: The developer's home/origin tenant where it was registered
explanation: The application object lives only in the tenant that registered it, and consuming tenants each get a service principal instead. The claim that it exists in every consenting tenant is the tempting reading of multi-tenant and is exactly wrong: one blueprint, many local instances, which is why the publisher edits permissions in one place.

prompt: A user consents to a third-party app requesting delegated access to their calendar. What exactly is being granted?
choices: The app may act as that user, within what they could do themselves
The app gains application-level access to every calendar in the whole tenant
The consent also grants admin consent for the entire tenant automatically
The app receives a client secret that only that user can see
correctAnswers: The app may act as that user, within what they could do themselves
explanation: One user consenting grants access to that user’s data and nothing more, which is why the risk of illicit consent scales with how many users can be tricked. The tenant-wide reading is the tempting fear and describes an application permission, whereas it would require an administrator to consent.

prompt: Which of these best distinguishes 'requested' permissions from 'granted' permissions for an application?
choices: Requested is declared on the registration; granted is consent on the SP
Requested and granted permissions are always identical and can never differ at all
Granted permissions are visible only in the Conditional Access sign-in logs
Requested permissions apply only to managed identities
correctAnswers: Requested is declared on the registration; granted is consent on the SP
explanation: The gap between the two is the whole point of consent: a registration can ask for anything, and only what was consented appears on the service principal. Believing they are always identical is the misconception that makes an app appear over-privileged in a review, whereas the requested list is a wish and the OAuth permission grants are the fact.

prompt: Four workload identity requirements. Assign the identity type that fits each; two entries in the list fit none of them.
sources: A service principal with a certificate
A service principal with a client secret

targets.label: One Azure Function needing its own identity, shared with no other resource
Fifty VMs that must all present the same identity, surviving any rebuild
A workload outside Azure, where a credential is unavoidable but should be strong
targets.correctSource: A service principal with a certificate

targets.label: A legacy script whose tooling can only present a password-style credential
targets.correctSource: A service principal with a client secret

explanation: The first two are decided by sharing and lifecycle: system-assigned is one-to-one and dies with its resource, user-assigned is standalone and shareable. The last two apply only where a managed identity is impossible — outside Azure — and there a certificate is preferred to a secret. The unused entries are not identity types at all: one is a consent record and the other governs sign-ins.

prompt: For each statement about delegated and application permissions, select Yes if it is true.

statements.text: Delegated permissions always require admin consent, whatever the scope.
Application permissions always require admin consent.
A delegated permission lets the app exceed what the signed-in user could do.
An application permission lets the app act with no signed-in user present.

explanation: The two types differ on one thing that then decides everything else: whether a user is in the flow. With a user, the user’s own access is the ceiling and low-risk scopes can be self-consented; without one, there is nobody to consent or to bound the access, so an administrator must approve it. The first statement is the common over-correction: treating all delegated permissions as admin-only removes the convenience the model is designed around, whereas only the higher-impact scopes need an administrator.

prompt: Complete the configuration that stops end users granting consent to new third-party apps while still letting legitimate requests reach a reviewer.

options: enable the admin consent workflow with named reviewers
disable the admin consent workflow entirely
require MFA for every sign-in in the tenant
assign every user the Application Administrator role
blanks.correctValue: enable the admin consent workflow with named reviewers

explanation: The two halves are one decision: blocking user consent without the workflow leaves users unable to work and unable to ask, which is how a hardening measure gets rolled back within a week. Disabling both is the tempting maximally-strict answer, whereas the named reviewers are what make the restriction survivable.

prompt: Which two statements about managed identities are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: System-assigned identities can be attached to multiple resources
Azure automatically rotates their credentials
User-assigned identities exist as standalone Azure resources
They require a client secret to be configured manually
correctAnswers: Azure automatically rotates their credentials
User-assigned identities exist as standalone Azure resources
explanation: System-assigned identities are strictly 1:1 and cannot be shared, and managed identities never require a manually configured secret at all.

prompt: Which two are true about application permissions (as opposed to delegated permissions)? (Choose two.)
choices: They always require admin consent before use
They act without any signed-in user context
They are scoped automatically to the consenting user’s own data
They can be consented to by any standard user in the tenant
correctAnswers: They always require admin consent before use
They act without any signed-in user context
explanation: The absence of a user is the cause and the admin-consent requirement is the consequence, so the two true statements are really one fact. Both false statements describe delegated behaviour, and the auto-scoping one is the more dangerous: it suggests an application permission is bounded by whoever consented, whereas it reaches the whole tenant.

prompt: Which two settings should typically be reviewed and hardened to reduce the risk of illicit consent grant attacks? (Choose two.)
choices: User consent settings, restricted to verified publishers
The admin consent workflow, with named reviewers for requests
Storage account public blob access on the subscription
Network security group inbound rules on the application subnet
correctAnswers: User consent settings, restricted to verified publishers
The admin consent workflow, with named reviewers for requests
explanation: Both settings govern who may agree to give an app access, which is the only surface this attack uses. The storage and NSG options are tempting because they are genuine hardening tasks, whereas an illicit consent grant crosses no network boundary and touches no storage account — the user simply clicks Accept.

prompt: Referring to requirement 2 (a nightly invoicing daemon with no signed-in user must read all mailboxes via Microsoft Graph, with access reviewable and visible to admins, not silently expandable by end users), which permission and consent configuration is correct?
choices: Mail.Read as an application permission, admin-consented and reviewed periodically
Mail.Read as a delegated permission, with each end user consenting individually
User consent enabled for all apps from any publisher, so that the daemon self-consents
The Global Administrator Entra role assigned to the service principal
correctAnswers: Mail.Read as an application permission, admin-consented and reviewed periodically
explanation: No user is present, so the permission must be the application form, and admin consent is what makes it visible and reviewable under Enterprise applications. Delegated with per-user consent is the tempting alternative and fails on the first clause rather than the last: an unattended nightly job has nobody to consent or to act as.

prompt: Referring to requirement 2, why is a delegated permission unsuitable for the nightly invoicing daemon?
choices: Delegated permissions need a signed-in user, which the daemon has not got
Delegated permissions are always more privileged than application permissions
Delegated permissions cannot be scoped to Mail.Read under any circumstances
Delegated permissions cannot be consented to by an administrator
correctAnswers: Delegated permissions need a signed-in user, which the daemon has not got
explanation: The daemon runs unattended, so there is no user for the app to act on behalf of and the token request has nothing to delegate. The claim that delegated permissions cannot be admin-consented is the tempting near-truth and is false — an administrator can consent to them on behalf of everyone, which still does not conjure a signed-in user at 2 a.m.

prompt: Referring to requirement 3 (the deployment pipeline on an Azure VM must retrieve a Key Vault secret with no client secret stored on the VM or in code), which identity approach is correct?
choices: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the VM and grant it a Key Vault RBAC role
Create a service principal with a client secret and store the secret in an environment variable on the VM
Embed the Key Vault master key directly in the pipeline's YAML file
Grant the VM's local administrator account access via a Key Vault access policy
correctAnswers: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on the VM and grant it a Key Vault RBAC role
explanation: A managed identity plus an RBAC role on the vault removes the credential entirely, which is what the requirement demands. Storing the client secret in an environment variable is the tempting alternative because it does work, whereas the secret is still on the VM — the requirement was not about connectivity but about nothing being stored.

prompt: Proposed solution: Register an app, request the Mail.Read application permission, obtain tenant-wide admin consent from a designated administrator, and periodically review the grant under Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: This is the standard pattern for an unattended job: an application permission with tenant-wide admin consent, visible and reviewable under Enterprise applications. Note the ongoing cost it accepts rather than avoids — the grant reaches every mailbox, so the periodic review is part of the control and not an optional extra.

prompt: Proposed solution: Register an app, request the Mail.Read delegated permission, and have the on-call engineer sign in interactively once a day to refresh the token for the background job. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: This still depends on a signed-in user and a delegated scope tied to that user, and is not a true unattended, admin-reviewable application-level grant — it's fragile and doesn't match the stated goal.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable user consent for all apps and permissions tenant-wide so the background job's service account can self-consent to Mail.Read the first time it runs. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Broad user consent lets grants expand silently without admin review, directly violating the requirement that access not be silently expandable by end users.

prompt: Order the steps an administrator follows to grant a daemon app admin-consented application permissions to Microsoft Graph.
reorderItems: Register the application under App registrations
Add the required application permission (e.g., Mail.Read) under API permissions
Verify the resulting grant under Enterprise applications ▸ Permissions
Periodically review the grant for continued need
explanation: The app must exist and declare the permission before anyone can consent to it, and the grant is verified afterwards on the service principal rather than on the registration. Consenting before adding the permission is the ordering mistake, whereas the review step is what stops the grant outliving the need for it.

prompt: Order the steps to move a VM-hosted workload from a service principal with a client secret to a managed identity.
reorderItems: Enable a system-assigned (or attach a user-assigned) managed identity on the VM
Grant the managed identity the required RBAC role on the target resource (e.g., Key Vault)
Update the application code to acquire tokens via the managed identity endpoint instead of a client secret
Remove the old client secret from configuration and revoke it on the service principal
Confirm the workload authenticates successfully with no stored secret remaining
explanation: The identity must exist and hold its role before the code can rely on it, and the old secret is revoked only after the new path is proven. Revoking the secret first is the ordering mistake that turns a migration into an outage, whereas leaving it forever is the other failure — a credential nobody uses is still a credential that works.

prompt: Configure this simplified API permissions screen for a nightly daemon app that must read all mailboxes with no signed-in user, ensuring the grant is properly consented at the tenant level.
explanation: A nightly daemon has no signed-in user, so the permission type must be Application and the grant must carry tenant-wide admin consent. The trap in this screen is the permission itself: the delegated and application forms share the name Mail.Read, whereas only the application form functions with nobody signed in.
